rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3, two-year field experiment (2017-2018) in a gray jujube orchard in Qiemo, Xinjiang, 12 plots, four treatments (T1 2 mm/d, T2 4 mm/d, T3 6 mm/d, CK), three replicates. Q2: Section 3.3 and Table 4: micro-sprinkler cooling significantly increased soluble sugar (2.7-6.5% in 2017, 2-4.3% in 2018) and yield of T2 and T3 (T2 highest, 6687 kg/hm2 in 2017, 6748 in 2018); Section 4.2 yield increased 1.87-7.35% versus control. Q4: Tables 1-3, Fig. 3, Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 measure the intermediate chain: air temperature/RH and VPD, leaf Pn, Tr, Gs, leaf WUE, and regress yield and soluble sugar against Pn (Fig. 6), with Section 4.3 linking VPD reductions to gas exchange via stomatal optimisation theory.
rows.notes: The claim row's technology field says 'drip' but the passage itself names micro-sprinkler irrigation, which is what the study tests (micro-sprinkler cooling applied on top of a drip-irrigated orchard); the study is not evidence for drip irrigation as such. Q3: yield, fruit quality and gas exchange each measured by a single method (harvest weighing, lab assays, LI-6400), no independent second method. Q5/Q6: one site, one crop, 500 m2 plots. Q7: effects stated as strongest at 4 mm/d and at flowering-fruit set, but these are treatment differences not stated requirements; yield gain for T3 was not significant in 2018. Q8: the explicit limitation (1-day leaf gas exchange record) concerns gas exchange, not yield; the remark that many other factors affect the Pn-yield relation is not framed as a limitation of the yield result, so rated no with doubt. Q9: Table 4 gives means with Duncan letter groups only, no SD/SE/CI for yield or sugar.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3, two-year field experiment in a gray jujube orchard with four micro-sprinkler treatments, three replicates, T/RH sensors at four heights. Q2: Section 3.1, Tables 1-3 and Fig. 3: micro-sprinkler cooling lowered mean air temperature by about 1.2-3.2 C and raised RH by 11-17% versus CK, mainly in the lower canopy, and reduced VPD from about 3 kPa to 2 kPa (Abstract; Fig. 3 VPD declines with sprayed amount). Q8: Section 4 (discussion preamble) states that leaf gas exchange (and the VPD values used in Fig. 3) come from a 1-day record and are not intended for water or carbon balance; Section 4.3 states VPD alone may not explain all aspects of stress and is used only as a null model; Section 4.3 also acknowledges the counter-argument that spraying could alter soil moisture. Q9: Fig. 3 caption reports values as mean <U+00B1> SE of three replicates for VPD, Pn, Tr and Gs.
rows.notes: The technology field says 'drip' but the passage names micro-sprinkler irrigation, which matches the study (micro-sprinkler cooling in a drip-irrigated orchard). Q3: air temperature and RH measured by one sensor type; VPD derived from the same measurements, so no independent method. Q4: the study measures the outcome variables (Ta, RH, VPD) and relates them to sprayed water amount but does not measure the evaporative cooling flux or energy balance through which the effect arises. Q5/Q6: single site, single crop, plot scale. Q7: effect stronger in lower canopy and with larger amounts, but no condition stated as a requirement from the study's own findings. Tables 1-3 give letter groups only; the SE in Fig. 3 supports Q9 for VPD.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The study is a two-year field experiment on micro-sprinkler cooling in a drip-irrigated gray jujube orchard in arid Xinjiang; both claim rows carry technology='drip' while the passage and the study concern micro-sprinkler irrigation, which may be a coding issue in the claim table rather than a study mismatch.
